🔻 Israeli attack, continued occupation of Lebanon will breach Iran-US MoU: Araghchi

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, referring to the Iran-US deal on ending the war, warns that any Israeli attack on Lebanon or the continued occupation of the territories of the Arab country ⁠will constitute a violation of the memorandum of understanding (MoU) between Tehran and Washington.

Araghchi’s warning came during his meeting with ambassadors, chargés-de-affaires, and heads of foreign and international missions residing in Tehran on Tuesday, where he briefed the gathering about the Iran-US negotiations aimed at ending the war launched by the United States and Israel against Iran in late February.
​
He said the MoU reached between Tehran and Washington, will take effect simultaneously with its official signing on Friday, adding that a new round of negotiations between the two sides to reach a final agreement will begin soon.
​
“In the first stage, the most important development is the declaration of the end of the war. Based on the decision we made, the end of the war was announced on Monday morning, once the final agreement was reached—Monday, Tehran time, of course. However, the memorandum will officially enter into force on Friday,” he explained.
​
The top diplomat further pointed to the connection between Lebanon and the Israeli aggression there to the joint Israeli-US war on Iran, saying the two fronts became somehow connected and dependent on each other.
​
Iran considered ending the war in Lebanon as a prerequisite for ending the war with Iran from day one, similar to a ceasefire that was declared on all fronts, with an emphasis on Lebanon, he said, adding that the two parties of the MoU are the United States and the Israeli regime on one side and Iran and Lebanon’s Hezbollah resistance movement on the other.
​
The objective of the deal will not be realized unless the war ends in Lebanon and Israeli forces withdraw from the territories they have occupied in this conflict, he emphasized, warning that any military attack and the continuation of the occupation from now on will be considered a violation of the memorandum.
​
Elsewhere, the foreign minister appreciated and thanked Pakistan and Qatar for their constructive role and efforts aimed at establishing peace and stability in the region.

The Peace Deal With No Text

The US and Iran agreed to stop shooting and restart the oil. The fine print doesn’t exist yet — at least not for the public.

Bloomberg reports that both sides have reached an interim agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and halt a war that has killed thousands and hammered global energy markets, with delegations due to meet in Switzerland on June 19 for a formal signing. 

But neither Washington nor Tehran has released the actual memorandum of understanding, and even officials admit that “some aspects of the deal remain unresolved,” leaving key disputes for the next round.

What we do know is narrow and fragile. The accord is built around a 60‑day window: an extended ceasefire, the phased reopening of Hormuz, limited sanctions relief and the start of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear program. 

Issues like enrichment levels, stockpiles of highly enriched uranium and the future of Iran’s missile and proxy capabilities are explicitly pushed into those talks, not settled by the deal itself. In other words, the guns mostly fall silent now so that arguments over the core problem can begin later.

That is why the truce looks so brittle. Previous leaks on the draft MOU already described it as “unrestricted” shipping and “no tolls” for 60 days, with Iran required to clear mines within roughly 30 days, and the US lifting its naval blockade in proportion to the return of commercial traffic. 

Iranian media, meanwhile, talk up their right to charge in future phases. Both sides are already telling different stories about the same corridor, before the first tanker even tests the route.

Bloomberg calls it what it is: a peace deal that ends active war and restarts oil flows, while explicitly deferring the most explosive files to a “next step” of 60‑day talks. 

A ceasefire built on an unpublished document and unresolved nuclear terms is less a settlement than a very expensive timeout.

Trump at G7: Selling a Deal, Leaving the Fine Print to Tehran

Trump arrived at the G7 looking like a tired salesman with one product left: the Iran deal he still can’t put on the table.

In Évian, he promised fellow leaders that Hormuz is practically open already, insisting “we have a lot of lanes right now” and calling the strait “open and toll‑free.” 

At the same time, Iranian outlets like Fars are briefing their public that any “free transit” is strictly time‑limited — 60 days, then Tehran reserves the right to charge, regulate and weaponize the chokepoint it just proved it can close. 

The president sells permanent relief; the other side advertises a paid trial period.

The White House message machine is working overtime to cover that gap. Talking points sent to surrogates stress that Trump “won’t hesitate” to resume strikes if Iran cheats, that “the pressure stays fully loaded,” and that there is “no open‑ended timeline” for Tehran to comply with the memorandum of understanding. 

That language is clearly aimed at nervous hawks who see the same problem critics do: the text of the deal is still secret, the timelines are fuzzy, and Washington is asking markets and allies to take it on faith that deterrence and verification are more solid than they look.

Meanwhile, global indicators are reacting to the headline, not the footnotes. Stocks are climbing, bonds are rallying, oil is slipping on the assumption that Hormuz will really reopen and stay open. 

Shipowners and insurers are less romantic: they remember previous presidential claims about “safe passage” that did not match what radar screens and risk models were telling them. 

Until the shooting stops in Lebanon and the rules in the strait are written, they know the true guarantor of security is not a G7 press spray but actuarial math.

Inside the summit hall, the subtext is even sharper. European leaders have already been talking about a world “less reliant on the U.S.” for security guarantees; now they are watching a war their ally started, could not finish on its own terms, and is trying to declare over via an interim memo whose nuclear and regional provisions are still undefined. 

Trump leans on the language of strength and flexibility; Iran leans on the leverage of a proven chokehold. Both sides say they’ve won. The only consensus so far is that no one is ready to show the actual contract.

So, at G7 level, this “victory” looks less like a new order and more like a managed climb‑down: an exhausted president arriving from a UFC birthday show at 3 a.m., promising that one more deal will fix the mess, while everyone in the room quietly plans for the day they may need protection from both the crisis and its cure.
